READING

**What the numbers actually say at the assessment date**

The pivot in PENDLARROW is the Marchwold grant. Everything else – taking Ardgowrie, hiring Kirstie, buying the vehicle – is justified on the promise of £100,000 coming back against the fit-out. So the first question is whether the 30 per cent threshold is genuinely met at the 2027-04-30 assessment.

The practice's own figure of 31.8 per cent is calculated "on last year's figures," meaning the FY2026 year-end base of £1,840,000 with the Ardgowrie annual value of £118,000 added and small animal left at £1,336,000. But the grant assessment does not read last year's figures. It reads "the annualised value of the work in force on that date" – which is a snapshot of what the practice is currently doing as of 30 April 2027, projected to a full year. That date is thirteen months after the FY2026 year-end. Small animal has been growing at 11 per cent a year for four consecutive years. Applying that rate over thirteen months:

£1,336,000 × 1.11^(13/12) ≈ £1,336,000 × 1.120 ≈ **£1,497,000**

Farm and equine at the same date:
- Base (flat for three years): £504,000
- Ardgowrie, in force and annualised: £118,000
- Total: **£622,000**

Annualised total in force: £622,000 + £1,497,000 = **£2,119,000**

Farm and equine share: £622,000 / £2,119,000 = **29.4 per cent**

The threshold is 30 per cent. The ratio lands approximately six-tenths of a point short. For the threshold to be met, small animal growth from April 2026 to April 2027 would need to slow from the four-year trend of 11 per cent to roughly 8 per cent. That is possible but cuts against a trend that has been stable for four years and which the practice is actively fuelling by opening Ordsall Green. The 31.8 per cent figure is arithmetically correct on the base used, but the base is thirteen months out of date by the time the assessor looks at it.

This matters because the grant is the load-bearing pillar of PENDLARROW's financial case. If it is not received, the practice has taken on £71,000 of annual vet salary, a £34,000 vehicle purchase, and a night-call commitment to 2030-04-30, in exchange for £118,000 of revenue whose gross contribution (£47,000 a year before vehicle depreciation, running costs, and any share of overhead) is financially modest.

**The night call-out question**

The outgoing practice held the Ardgowrie contract for nine years, not nine months. Nine years is a long time to make something work. The stated reason on the handover call was the night call-out load. That is not a complaint about the client or the cattle; it is a description of an operational burden that a practice with experienced farm vets eventually found unsustainable. Kirstie Ballantyne-Rowe is willing to move with the contract, and that is genuinely valuable – continuity of care, no cold start, client relationship already in place. But she was part of the team that just returned the contract. Her willingness to join Wrentham Cross does not resolve why her current employer gave it up.

If Kirstie handles the nights and finds them as demanding as the outgoing practice did, the question becomes whether £71,000 including all on-costs is adequate compensation over time. If she leaves within a year or two, Wrentham Cross has to cover 900 dairy cattle out of its existing team, build a night rota from scratch, or surrender the contract. Surrendering the contract triggers full repayment of £100,000. The practice would then have paid for the grant risk entirely in the form of the repayment, while having lost the vet and the revenue.

**The grant tail risk**

Even if the grant is received and Kirstie stays, the herd health contract must be held continuously until 2030-04-30 – three and a half years after the contract starts. The Ardgowrie cattle are 900 dairy cows, which means regular night emergencies (calvings, milk fever, displaced abomasums) and an on-call obligation that does not reduce over time. The practice is committing itself to carrying that obligation for over three years as a condition of keeping £100,000 it will already have spent. A practice that builds small animal and walks away from farm work in 2028 because the ratio no longer makes sense would be forced either to maintain a contract it has no strategic reason to keep, or to repay the grant at that point.

**Cash position**

Under either course, the fit-out of £260,000 is paid from the £310,000 on deposit, leaving £50,000 in cash. Under PENDLARROW, the vehicle is a further £34,000 capital purchase, taking cash to £16,000 before the grant arrives. The grant is claimed after the April 2027 assessment, so the cash trough occurs from roughly November 2026 (contract start, vehicle needed) through to late Q2 2027 at the earliest. £16,000 of headroom against a practice with a fifteen-person payroll and two premises is thin. The Ardgowrie contract generates approximately £9,800 a month in revenue against £5,900 in vet salary, so the monthly cash from the contract itself is positive from day one, but there is no buffer for anything unexpected in the fit-out, the vehicle, or the practice more widely.

Under WESTERGATE, £50,000 remains after the fit-out. No grant, no vehicle, no additional vet hiring immediately for farm work. The next hire goes into small animal, where it supports revenue that has been growing at 11 per cent per year and where Ordsall Green will generate demand that needs clinical capacity.

**The Ardgowrie economics in isolation**

If the grant is set aside, Ardgowrie contributes:
- Revenue: £118,000
- Vet cost: £71,000
- Gross contribution: £47,000 (39.8 per cent margin)
- Less vehicle depreciation (say £5,000–6,000/year on a five-year write-down) and running costs
- Net contribution in the region of £40,000/year

Over the 3.5 years to the grant lock-in end that is roughly £140,000. That is a real number, but it is the return on an operational commitment that requires a dedicated vet, a vehicle, 24/7 on-call for 900 dairy cattle, and a grant repayment risk hanging over it the entire time. It is not obviously wrong to take that deal, but it is not obviously right either, and the financial case depends heavily on the grant which is itself doubtful.

**The small animal trajectory**

Small animal at 11 per cent per year:
- FY2027: £1,483,000
- FY2028: £1,647,000
- FY2029: £1,828,000
- FY2030: £2,029,000

Ordsall Green is being fitted out precisely to capture this growth. The building investment is already committed. Putting the next hire into small animal is not sacrificing something; it is staffing the business whose growth is funding the practice. The farm and equine book, flat for three years, is not going to reverse that trajectory. WESTERGATE does not abandon farm and equine – the existing team keeps what it has – but it does not ask the practice to bet its cash and operational capacity on holding a night-call contract for four years in order to recoup £100,000 that may not in fact be payable.

**Where this leaves the two courses**

PENDLARROW has three compounding risks: the grant threshold is probably not met at the assessment date once small animal growth is accounted for; if the grant is received, it is held at risk until 2030 against a night-call burden that ended the previous nine-year relationship; and the cash position after fit-out and vehicle is £16,000. The contract economics without the grant are positive but modest.

WESTERGATE costs the practice the £47,000 annual Ardgowrie contribution and the £100,000 grant, but the grant is conditional on a threshold the practice probably cannot meet, and the £47,000 contribution comes with the operational obligations attached. The practice keeps £50,000 in cash, keeps its hiring capacity pointed at small animal, and carries no grant repayment liability to 2030.

The decisive question is not whether the outgoing practice's night-call experience will be repeated – it may not be. The decisive question is whether the financial case for PENDLARROW stands up before that risk is even run, and on the grant arithmetic it does not.

---

READING
  The 31.8 per cent eligibility figure is calculated on FY2026 small-animal revenue of £1,336,000, but the grant assessment occurs on 2027-04-30, thirteen months later. Applying the stated four-year trend of eleven per cent annual small-animal growth gives an annualised small-animal figure at the assessment date of approximately £1,497,000. Farm and equine with Ardgowrie is £622,000. Total annualised work in force: approximately £2,119,000. Farm-and-equine share: approximately 29.4 per cent. The grant threshold is 30 per cent. The eligibility calculation presented for PENDLARROW freezes small-animal revenue at the FY2026 year-end figure; the assessment does not. For the threshold to be met, small-animal growth would need to slow from 11 per cent to roughly 8 per cent over the next thirteen months, cutting against a four-year trend the practice is actively reinforcing with the Ordsall Green fit-out. If the grant is not received, PENDLARROW delivers: a dedicated farm vet at £71,000 per year, a £34,000 vehicle purchase, a night-call obligation on 900 dairy cattle running to 2030, and a gross contract contribution of approximately £47,000 a year before depreciation and running costs – all funded from a post-fit-out cash position of £16,000. That is not a strong position. The separate operational risk – that the reason the outgoing practice handed back a nine-year contract was precisely the night-call load that Wrentham Cross would now carry, and that the incoming vet was part of the team that reached that conclusion – compounds the financial uncertainty without resolving it. WESTERGATE leaves £50,000 in cash after the fit-out, directs the next hire into the business growing at 11 per cent a year, and carries no grant repayment liability. The forgone contribution and the forgone grant are both real costs, but the grant is contingent on arithmetic the practice probably cannot satisfy, and the contribution is attached to obligations whose sustainability the outgoing practice already tested to breaking point.

CALL
  WESTERGATE

GROUNDS
  The 31.8 per cent eligibility figure holds the small-animal denominator at the FY2026 year-end level, but the assessment reads the work in force thirteen months later, by which point eleven-per-cent annual small-animal growth carries the ratio to approximately 29½ per cent, below the 30 per cent threshold, removing the grant that is PENDLARROW's primary financial justification, while the night-call burden that ended a nine-year relationship at the outgoing practice remains unresolved and is now a four-year commitment backed by a £100,000 repayment obligation.
